goal: Deploy the status-page web service in a way the small team can sustain over time.
question: Select the deployment target for the containerized status-page service: a managed platform, a self-managed server, or another materially different hosting approach.
known_constraints: The service is a small containerized status web service (README.md).
The team can afford either a managed platform or a small virtual server, so cost alone is not disqualifying (README.md).
One person can handle server upkeep, and there is no on-call rotation (README.md).
The team has stated no strong deployment preference yet (README.md).

environment.app: Single-file Python 3.12 standard-library HTTP server returning a constant 'status: ok' body on 0.0.0.0:8080 (app.py:6-14).
environment.packaging: Docker image based on python:3.12-slim; no HEALTHCHECK and no TLS configuration (Dockerfile).
environment.repository: Three files total (README.md, app.py, Dockerfile); no CI/CD, reverse proxy, TLS, or infrastructure-as-code configuration present (file listing checked 2026-10-02).
environment.operations: One maintainer available for server upkeep; no on-call rotation (README.md).

evidence: The app serves a constant body 'status: ok' over plain HTTP on 0.0.0.0:8080 using only the Python standard library (app.py:6-14).
The Dockerfile packages the app as a python:3.12-slim container and defines no HEALTHCHECK or TLS termination (Dockerfile).

README states the team can afford either a managed platform or a small virtual server, one person can handle server upkeep, there is no on-call rotation, and there is no strong preference yet (README.md:3-5).
The repository contains no CI/CD pipeline, reverse proxy config, TLS certificates, or infrastructure-as-code files (file listing checked 2026-10-02).

alternatives.name: Managed Container Platform
alternatives.description: Deploy the existing Docker image to a managed container platform that builds from the repository, provides an HTTPS endpoint with managed TLS, and restarts the container automatically.
advantages: No server upkeep: OS patching, runtime upgrades, and TLS renewal are handled by the platform
Automatic restarts and platform health checks replace on-call intervention for common failures
Deployments can be triggered from git or CI without manual server steps
disadvantages: Recurring platform fee with pricing that can vary with usage
Runtime is constrained to what the platform supports, and some configuration is platform-specific
Less visibility into and control over the host environment
assumptions: A platform that runs python:3.12-slim containers is available and accepts this image
The team is willing to create a platform account and configure a deployment pipeline

alternatives.name: Self-Managed Virtual Server
alternatives.description: Run the existing Docker image on a small virtual server that the team operates, with Docker for the container and a reverse proxy added for TLS.
advantages: Full control over the host, network, and runtime configuration
Flat and predictable monthly cost for a small instance
Runs the existing Dockerfile unchanged with standard tooling
disadvantages: OS patching, TLS certificate renewal, and proxy configuration are manual and fall on one maintainer
With no on-call rotation, outages wait until that person is available
A single server is a single point of failure unless redundancy is added later
assumptions: The team provisions and pays for a small virtual server
A reverse proxy or equivalent is added for TLS, since the app serves plain HTTP on port 8080

alternatives.name: Static Hosting behind a CDN
alternatives.description: Publish the status response as a static file on managed static hosting with a CDN, replacing the Python server with a static page.
advantages: No server and no container runtime to maintain at all
CDN edge delivery keeps the page reachable under load
Costs are typically at or below small-container pricing for a single page
disadvantages: Requires changing the deliverable: the Python service is replaced by a static page, so app.py and the Dockerfile are no longer the runtime
Any future dynamic checks, such as probing other systems, would need a new mechanism
Deployment becomes a build-and-upload step instead of running the service
assumptions: The current response body is constant ('status: ok'), so a static page reproduces the service today
The team accepts treating the status page as a static artifact rather than a running service

criteria.name: Operational burden
rubric: Regular manual upkeep required with no on-call coverage

criteria.name: Availability and incident response
rubric: Failures wait on a single maintainer to notice and fix
Failures auto-restart but recovery paths are manual
Platform-managed recovery with automatic restarts and failover

criteria.name: Fit with existing artifact
rubric: Requires replacing the current service implementation
Requires extra components or pipeline work before the service runs
Runs the existing Docker image as-is

criteria.name: Cost fit
rubric: Cost likely exceeds what the team can afford
Cost is affordable but varies with usage

criteria.name: Control and portability
rubric: Fully proprietary runtime with artifact lock-in
Full control over host and portable artifacts

criteria.name: TLS and patching posture
rubric: Manual TLS and patching owned by the team
